title: LB Jordan Burch Press Conference 07-09-26 | Arizona Cardinals 2026
text: During this time last year, you're getting ready for your first camp. In what ways is your two Jordan Birch different than year one? >> I kind of know what to expect going in and then like knowing what to look for and then talking to Feeney, he kind of like told me what to plan for for the off season. So, I feel like it'll go a lot better than it did last year. >> How beneficial was it to actually have an off season because when you're coming into your rookie year, you're doing so much of the draft prep stuff. So, how different was it maybe to actually just focus in on what the coaches are saying here? >> Yeah, I don't think anything was like a surprise. I kind of know what to prep for. So, this off season I know like look at my old plays and then I can call my coach and tell him like from last year to this year what what does he want to see on the field. >> Going into your first coaching change, head coach, position coach, what what have you kind of learned about maybe what new coaches ask of you or what new things are you going to be asked to do this year? >> Um, it's really like they just want the best out of you. So, just going into it, they're they're watching film from last year but they know what I can critique and what I can do better at. I mean it's not a it's not a lot. They know like what's the best for me. So, I just, you know, ask every question I can to get the best out of me. >> What are some of the areas that you want to do improve this off season? >> Um, really my pass rush and then a lot of like our position is dropping and knowing what kind of routes you're going to get. So, last year I didn't really know much about it. So, now I can like hone in on like the main things of our position. >> The the front office didn't bring in many other pass rushers to that room. Do you think that that says kind of something about how far you guys are trying to be coming along throughout this throughout this off season? >> I feel like they trust our group and then like our progress coming into this new season. I feel like we've been getting better every day and it kind of shows, you know, out on the [snorts] field and in the film room. So, I think I think they trust us a little bit more. >> How big of an influence has Josh Sweat been on you? >> Um, a lot. Like he's I mean he he might be quiet around the building but like that's one of the funniest guys on the team. Um and like any question I can ask about pass rush or like what I what I should do against a O-line, he'll help me out. So, um coming from him, it means a lot. >> What would probably What would you probably say was maybe the biggest surprise or takeaway from your first season in the league? >> Probably match-ups. [snorts] Um like every every week, every game you're going to get somebody good. Um and then like the talent of like the quarterbacks. Like we playing the Rams, like how quick they get the ball out. Just like different things like that was like the biggest surprise for me rookie year. >> There's a lot of talk about what this pass rush room could do, what it could look like. Do you guys feel like I mean I know you said that there's trust there and that's obviously important. Within the room, does it feel like there's pressure to actually deliver on that trust even more so than maybe last year? >> Um I wouldn't say pressure, but I can feel like at practice everybody's kind of like putting it together. Like from last year to this year, we're kind of like clicking, laughing together, like helping each other out on the field. So, I feel like um we'll we'll do a lot better this year coming up. >> What was uh some of the things you were really happy with yourself last year? >> Uh I think my progress throughout the season. Um so, like a lot of things I didn't really understand, but like throughout I was kind of like gaining more confidence in being on the field and being able to do it. >> What do you think about just the general like outside of work here? Like what did you learn about the area, getting acclimated to things here and all that? >> Um everybody's nice around here. It's hot, so I had to get >> [laughter] >> I had to get used to that, but I mean everybody's nice and uh helpful. Um I mean it's a great great place to live. >> What have been some of the things you've been doing outside of football this off season? >> Um I have I try to have the guys over sometimes. Um and like we'll like eat dinner or like watch TV or something like that. Other than that, we're we're either on the game. So, I haven't really done much. I'm trying to get into golf, but you know, still trying to figure it out. >> Have you been paying attention to the World Cup at all, or are you interested in that? >> Uh a little bit last week. I really haven't been watching much of it.

So, I'm not even considering keeping an extra guy there. I mean, you know, I I like what I saw. Holland seems like an older, more expensive player that could show the effects of age. Alternatively, how could there not be room for Booty when there is for Pop and Chisum?" Before that, he didn't really do much of anything. And in fact, um, at this time last year heading into camp, I would say the consensus internally on Kahan Booty was I don't think he's going to make it. I don't think he's going to make the team. But credit to him, credit to Todd Downing, the receivers's coach, for the development that Kahan Booty showed. he was um consistent and improved during um training camp through the season, you know, all that stuff. So, um he definitely defied predictions, expectations, even internal ones um for the past year. M Now, M. Holland, uh M. Holland, first of all, the guy's in phenomenal shape. I don't know if you've seen any of his workout videos, what he's doing. The guy's a beast. Um, he's a really good player. He's different. He gives you a lot more, um, length, um, catch radius. Uh, he blocks like a son of a gun. He plays special teams. Booty's average at best blocker. Doesn't play any special teams. He's shorter. Um, I don't know if Booty's any more explosive than M. Collins maybe, but um and then room for booty. No room for booty, but there is for pop and chisum. Well, pop and chisum are their quote unquote well and dos. Um I would say that Dobs and Chisum are more of classic slot players for the PA Patriots and Chisum blocks, loves the block. um certainly blocks well I would say for his size I don't think Booty would do that if you say put him inside say Pop Douglas is a space player the Patriots don't have much speed I would say that you know on my 53 let me just find it um in terms of like speed guys it's Williams and Douglas and do you want a slow plotting offense I think they're trying to move beyond that and so uh if it's close I'm going with speed, explosiveness. Um, so that's sort of my rationale at uh receiver, tight end, fullback. Last year, three, I am keeping three. Um, four now. Hunter Henry, Reggie Gilliam at fullback, Eli Raridan as the third guy. Um, I did have Tanner Arkin, undrafted rookie Hback on my initial Oh, 53. I just, [clears throat] excuse me, I decided that there was decent chance that they could get him to the practice squad. Are those guys really going to get claimed on 53? Probably no. Could get stolen to a practice squad. Um, that can always, you know, happen. But, um, you know, Arkin is definitely a guy that I want to see more of. I think he's part, if not the entire reason why they have not made a veteran signing to replace Julian Hill. We knew that they went into this wanting a Julian Hill. I would say that Tanner Arin more than CJ Dippy has more of a chance to fill that Julian Hill role. It's going to be a lot as a rookie. I understand. Uh but I think he deserve I want to see what he can do before I do anything. So that's my uh that's my thinking there. Okay. So what's next on the list? Okay. We have offensive line. I group them into tackles and guard center. At tackle last year they have four. This year I have five. I did the opposite at guard center. Last year they had five. I have four. Um I do have a trade at offensive tackle. I have Marcus Bryant going out. That's I mean look I have obviously you have for now you have the two tack two starting tackles Will Campbell Morgan Moses Caleb Lomu is the third offensive tackle. Um, it could easily be Hudson and Bryant could easily swap spots where Bryant beats him out and Hudson is now trade bait. I think that you should be able to get something for a tackle that shows something. I think that they have in Crownover Hudson and Bryant. I think they have guys that can play in this league. Um, and so that's my thinking there. at guard center. Obviously, you have Michael Wenu, Jared Wilson, Elijah Vera Tucker, and Ben Brown. Those guys are pretty much locked and loaded. I think he could get to the practice squad. I just think as of right now, and again, we haven't seen these guys in pads, so a lot is going to change a week into camp as far as our evaluations of the offensive line, defensive line, edge players, tight end, blocking tight ends, all that stuff when they actually do it in practice. Um, I just don't see anybody worthy on that list of keeping. And, uh, I would rather leave that spot open. Maybe I'm claiming somebody from another team. what have you. Um, you know, but and maybe that changes the numbers on the offensive line, but that's sort of where I am uh right now. Let's see if there are any other questions. Um, so I think this is related. Uh, well, I did mention in my column that uh I don't totally rule out a Morgan Moses trade. Um, and Packers Boy took did not really agree with that. Greg not so sure on the Moses idea of a trade. They still need this experience, his experience, and let Lomu gain experience and transition to a starter next year. Um, yes, in theory. I would say as of right now, the odds are much stronger that he needs almost a full developmental year and Morgan Moses is the starter. I'm allowing for the possibility that Caleb Lomu comes in and at some point when the pads go on and over the course of the summer and the preseason games that Caleb Lomu as a firstround pick looks like one of their best five offensive linemen. And when you consider that when you consider Morgan Moses's age when and you know you could make the argument that like well just keep Morgan Moses just in case something happens and um yeah that's fine and he might be okay with that because he's been a terrific leader for the Patriots but as we've seen this regime kind of when it when guys get supplanted when veterans get supplanted by younger cheaper players players. So, if Caleb Blumu comes in and all of a sudden catches fire and he looks like an NFL starting offensive tackle and say those other offensive tackles like I talked about, you know, whether it's um whether it's uh Crownover, Hudson, Bryant, th if those guys want at least one of those guys to to to elevate Lommo to a starter to trade Morgan Mos Moses, one of those younger guys, it's not just about Lomu, one of those younger guys is going to have to prove or get to the point where the Patriots say he can handle it if Lomu or Will Campbell goes down. That has to happen. I don't rule that out. I'm not saying I prefer that. I don't. Um, and maybe the Patriots were so scarred by last year that they're like, "We're going to keep all tackle options because we don't know what's going to happen." And that's certainly possible, but I think that um I I'm just leaving the possibility open that that could happen, that Morgan Moses could be traded. I'm not saying it's at all likely. I'm just keeping it open, that's all. And I think they're this is so somewhat related my Cronin 127. Do you think the Patriots will use more power formations on offense as opposed to the recent bias towards 13 personnel, one tight end, three wide receivers? Just my opinion, I think the extra running back and extra tight end fullback at the expense of a wide receiver and the third quarterback would make more sense given my assumption that they would want to play more power football. Um, I just think, look, I I think it's obvious that they want to play more power football. They signed Julian Hill. They signed Reggie Gillian. They also signed Elijah Vera Tucker. They want to get better running the ball. They want to be able to get heavier. They want to be able to do different things and win an offense in different ways and not just rely on Drake May and you know and the receivers. That's no way to live. Not if you want to win big in this league. Um so it's obvious they want to do that. Now as far as affecting roster composition, a lot of this is sort of what I talked about earlier. I think a lot of these position he mentioned extra running back and extra tight end fullback. I think those are positions that aren't um they're not prioritized around the league. So I think you can pretty much get away with um providing building depth on the practice squad. So you don't necessarily have to change the 53. And also I talked about the quarterback. I mean, it a lot of it depends on Morton, but I think it's obvious that they wanted to get a young understudy in here, get into the Josh McDaniel system, let him be trained up so in, you know, a year from now, two years from now, he's ready to be the backup um to Drake May. So, um I think that's where we are. So, I'm going to end it there. Thanks for tuning in. Uh hope everybody enjoyed it. Um I will be back probably next week. we can go over defense and some other things. title: The DiCecco Daily Special: Ifeanyi Momah Thought He "Made It" When The Eagles Signed Him, Until ...
text: [music] Hello and welcome in everyone to another episode of the Czecho Daily, but it's a special edition of the Czecho Daily. Why? Because I'm joined by former Eagles wide receiver Afani Mom, who's kind enough to join me. And Afani, how's it how's it going, man? Thanks for uh carving out a few minutes. >> Yeah, it's my pleasure, man. Thanks for inviting me. Um, all is well, you know, all is well. I'm doing good on this end. >> Great to hear. But before we get into your foray into Eagles training camp where you spent two seasons, first, how did you wind up in Philadelphia? >> Yeah. Uh, my story was unique. Um, you know, this and a long time ago as well, but you know, my senior year at Boston College, first game of the season, I tore my ACL against Northwestern, unfortunately. and was really banking on that year to make some noise to get me, you know, at least signed to an NFL team. Years prior to that were decent, but not enough. You know, I really needed that senior year tape. So, when that didn't come through, um, you know, I retired, missed my rookie, missed that season and missed my rookie year. And after two years away from football, I was like, man, I still got an itch. I want to see what I can do. So, worked out and did proday at BC as a vet, you know, as a as a free agent. And that's kind of how I got on the radar. And you know, I was picking between a few teams, but I landed with the Eagles just cuz I really I really liked what Chip Kelly stood for um at that time. And you know, he was he was uh um the coach of my receivers's coach at Boston College um who coincidentally is Ryan Day um who's crushing right now with uh Ohio State. So um you made a lot of sense at the time. I wanted to go somewhere where I had some familial ties and um you know a team me that was interested that made sense and and that's how I kind of ended up in Philly. >> So you joined the Eagles and you alluded to this at the start of the Chip Kelly era. What were your initial impressions about his offense? >> Yeah, it was unlike anything I ever seen before. I I started playing football at seven. Um I love football. I'm 6'7. Most people say why don't I play basketball? I was I have told the brothers and I just fell in love with the game. So you know I've been around football for a long time and played in many different offenses. um many many many different offenses and I never seen an offense like that one. Um and you know it was intriguing. You know I felt like it was like kind of like track on turf. You know you have an offense where you you can get some guys who buy into the system um who are athletes and you know I think it could be something that's kind of where my my mindset was is like this is something unique and something I never seen before and he's had great success. So I bought in man. I wanted to really, you know, utilize my skill set and, you know, buy into the to the process and see what can happen. And, um, and yeah, I think I he's had he had great success when he was there and not some not so much great times, but some some really good times um, initially when he was there. >> So, your first summer was in 2013. Did you have a welcome to the NFL moment? >> Oh, man. Um, I would say nothing crazy. the the one situation I remember well um you know I I ran a 4-3 in my proday and you know I have some really good numbers um and I'm 67 and there's a lot of hype behind me right when I signed with the Eagles I think I had like 15,000 people follow me on Twitter at that time it was a lot of people um and you know when I sign when I got to um you know OTAAS and and you know incorporated with the vets I was behind Deshawn Jackson I was in the two deep um And when we got to training camp, you know, first day training camp, I we got to one-on ones and we were doing drills, you know, reps that counted, right? Everybody's watching. We're competing. Um DJ went and then I'm getting ready to go and realize Ben jumped in front of me and I'm like, "All right, whatever." And then after a AB went, um I think it was uh my boy BJ. BJ jumped in front of me. Everybody was just cutting me and me being like, you know, I've been out of for two years. I ain't really know what I was doing. I'm kind of nervous. I was kind of was letting it happen, you know. I was letting people cut me. I'll never forget after that practice Jeremy Mul. I said, "Oh man, you in the 2D. Don't let people do that to you, man. You got to, you know, fight fight for what's yours." So, you know, I don't think I really had any moments outside of that where, you know, you hear the some of these stories like, "Welcome to football." A guy has to pay a crazy bill at dinner or, you know, got to carry a vets pad or you have get get blown up by somebody. Um, I could definitely talk about getting blown up blown up by somebody. But in the initial year, that was kind of my like, all right, like I'm a pro. I gotta handle myself like a business. Nobody's gonna come, you know, and push for me except for myself and vouch for myself. So, you know, I got to really go out there and get it every day against these grown men who are trying to feed their families um and competing um the way that they think they should compete. So, I got to match that energy. So, that was kind of my moment. and and you mentioned the hype and how many followers you got since signing with the Eagles uh back in 2013. It's pretty become common place that when you see bigbodied wide receivers, they tend to uh draw a lot of intrigue from the outside. What do you remember from that period when that interest was really building? >> Yeah, I mean it was a while ago, but one thing really stood out to me. I was at my mom's house. I was helping her clean the house and obviously talking to my agent, my my brother um just about what to do. And when uh I told my agent I want to go with Philly and the news got out there um you know I was back in my mom's living room. I look at my phone and had my phone was just non-stop just dinging ding ding ding ding notifications coming through. Social media going crazy. Um, you know, I remember that thought of like, yeah, like this is pretty cool, you know, like I'm not I made it and I was wrong, you know, but that that thought of like, all right, like I went from, you know, getting my ACL surgery and going to master's classes cuz, you know, I was a fifth year student and thinking football was over and, you know, basically two years later it's like, you know, it actually happened, you know, this is pretty cool and and Um, you know, I don't really have people in my family or my network at that time that were, you know, former NFL players or current NFL players. So, I just didn't know what to do. You know, I couldn't pick up the phone and call some of these vets from Boston College like Matt Ryan or anything. I wasn't getting drafted, you know, so I just went out there and figured it out. But, it was just one of those situations where um, you know, after so much time off, it felt pretty cool to at least get some recognition. And I knew that there's a lot more work that needed to go in, but I sat back for a little bit and smelled the flowers at that at that time >> because there was so much buzz. Did you at any point feel any additional pressure because of it? >> Oh, yeah. Here and there. I'll say I I'm a very, you know, I'm a I'm a competitive guy, you know, and I I like to say like I don't like to fail, you know, so um I had enough pressure that I put on myself and I'm not big on social media. I've deleted my Twitter and Instagram multiple times and made new ones and you know, I would say that wasn't bad. you know, the pressure from fans or even the coaches. I just I was very critical and harsh on myself. And I think uh that was the hard part was like getting through that mental block. And you know, you it's true. Like I think as a rookie, as a young player, a lot of these guys, you see it today and you've seen it years and years and years in the past. Like it takes a little while for rookies and young players to really adjust. And the ones that adjust quickly are it's it's a it's a rare that's a rare breed. That's a rare situation. So, I think for me, um, looking back and reflecting on it, my first year, two years, I definitely was very hard on myself. I had a lot to learn. Um, and and I would say nobody really was putting pressure more on myself than I was putting on myself, you know. >> What are what are some of the challenges that a bigger bodied wide receiver faces that maybe some wouldn't realize? Yeah, I would say uh I mean we all know it's football, you know, it's it's it's there's a lot of people on the field and it's hard to dictate how things go for you when you're playing receiver, tight end, all the different positions where you're not controlling the ball or you're not touching the ball, throwing the ball. And um you know I would say like that aspect um really makes it it makes it unique in the sense of like um you can really have a lot of advantages set up for yourself but it's hard to exploit it. It's hard to utilize it. It's hard to put it on display. Um, but I would say just being a a receiver in that specific position, it's very hard to like get in and out of cuts and be fast enough to get separation from a guy who's quicker, you know, more agile. Um, and in a in a system where, you know, you'll be on the outside and, you know, working with some space, but you got to really learn how to create separation. That was a little hard for me to adjust to. Um, but I think that's one of those things where, you know, if you know how to play the game and and utilize, you know, the system that you're in, watch film, try to exploit certain things, um, hopefully have a offensive coordinator who's doing that. Uh, which I felt like I we did, but, you know, I never really got to I didn't not make it to the regular season to really try to, you know, match up against the team and utilize my size against them. We had big receivers anyways, right? Riley Cooper at that time, 6'4. Um, Jeremy Mlin, Jason Avon, you know, I think the smallest guy was was DJ. Um, so we have big receivers. I think for me, I was just trying to learn from them on how to do the things that really mattered, right, for that were harder for most tall receivers. Create separation. Um, you know, be kind of a possession guy, but it's easier for us to go and get the ball, right? Play basketball and turf because we're taller guys. So, but just creating separation, I think, was the hardest thing as a outside receiver. Um, and I think that kind of went hand in hand with when I did have success in the league and I moved from receiver to tight end and started playing inside. So, >> now the Eagles have uh legendary wide receiver Harold Carmichael often around. Um, I believe he was 6'7, maybe even taller than that. >> Oh, yeah. >> Did you have any conversations with Harold about it? >> Yeah, many conversations. I'm not sure what Harold's capacity is today as far as his involvement um with the Eagles and their practices and being around on the field and stuff. Um but when I was with the Eagles in 2013 and 14, Harold was on the field. You know, he was around. He had gloves on. He was every day around and and being active. And um you know, he was a phenomenal player. The guy was incredible and he was a great resource. Um and very friendly. You know, really really was rooting for me. Um I think a lot of the hype around me being 67 and being on the Eagles was because of our history um with Harold, you know, I was like, "Hey, the next is this next Harold Carmichael." And I thought that was pretty cool. And getting to meet him and see him and watch his film um you know, really every every chance that I had to learn more about him, I was more intrigued, more impressed. You know, he was incredible. So, um it was truly a blessing being able to be with the Eagles at that time and being around Harold um to learn from him and and get his support, you know. Was there ever a moment in those two summers where you felt like, you know, I belong here and I have an opportunity to to make this roster? >> Yeah, off and on. Off and on. I I definitely went through the ringer of like, yeah, I belong. I could do this. And I had that moments where I was like, man, I stink. I I don't know if I'm going to make this team, let alone if I'm cut out for the NFL. And I think anybody who's gone through this the struggle of you know success and failure in the NFL which I mean every player I think goes through that you you might question yourself and go through that u that stuff. I would say for me um I had some really good practices you know two-minute drills scoring touchdowns things like that. Um and some pre good good preseason games making a couple catches here and there. Um but the the size where I was like man I don't think I'm cut out for the situations where like you know I remember I think it was year one or year two I don't know if it was 13 or 14 against the Eagles when you know that first drive I ended up I think it was the first play I caught a little 5 yard in and um took about two steps and got smacked to fumble the ball and then um you know had like two catches after that and then later on in that first quarter I we're in the red zone and I ran it in and I caught the ball landed and it popped out you know just crazy things like that where it's like you know it's just you wish it went differently and I was very sensitive at that time as far as like when something bad happens it's hard for me to shake it off. So, um, yeah, I had those highs and lows and you know, I think it's a part of the what makes football great and you know what makes those great players great is being able to just forget when a bad play happens because it's football. You're playing against the best of the best. Guys are going to mess up all the time, you know, and I think the absolute greatest players learn how to adjust quickly and not focus on the last play and move on to the next and, you know, try to try to, you know, continue to strive for success on the field. So >> from from a mental perspective, how did you eventually learn how to push past some of those, you know, uh me bouts of adversity when things weren't going your way? Uh did you lean on anybody? Was it something inherent that that allowed you to do that? >> Yeah. Um I definitely lean on on a few people. Um I'll just mention uh my family. My brothers are big in my life. They were my big supporters. Um and and I was just going to them with everything, you know. Um, and the the big the big piece was Aurelius Ben. Um, he was a vet to me. I would say he was like my bigger brother. He took me in. He saw when I was having some hard times. He saw that and, you know, invited me to his house, have dinner with his family and just talked to me, you know, kind of helped me get my mind off football and just kind of res hit reset um before going back in the building the next day. And, um, that relationship continued throughout the years. you know, I I would train with him in the offseasons and, you know, got really really close with him. So, he was a big piece of helping me just adjust to the speed of the game, the mentality, what it takes. Um, and and I I really appreciate him cuz it was definitely hard times my first year just adjusting and learning and also being around big name players, right? Michael Vic was around, Nick, >> Sanchez, Markley, we had some really good players in that building and you know, coaches, um, Howie Roseman, you know, the Eagles bring a certain level of stardom, I would say, um, every year. Um, and so when you get the chance to be on that team, be in that building, being around these people, you know, it's definitely one of those opportunities where, you know, you kind of kick yourself like, man, this is real. You know, I'm here. I'm doing it and I'm around some really, really cool people. >> how about from a team building standpoint? Did you did you remember any rookie talent shows or did you guys go out and do anything to kind of build that chemistry? >> Um, yeah. For me, it was unique because I I really didn't have a rookie season, you know. I never got Hayes. I never got I came in the league and I was considered a vet just because I um I didn't I didn't kind of get grouped in with the rookie class. And I my maybe it was my doing, you know, because I was technically a a rookie on paper, but it just had instead of, you know, you pull up the roster and it'll say either R or say one year for a guy hasn't hasn't played yet. And I was fortunate not to have the R and I had the one year. Um, and I was telling guys, you know, I'm I'm a free agent that just signed. I didn't tell them I was a rookie. So, I didn't get have to participate in any hazing, rookie singing, anything like that. But definitely have seen um a few different rookie hazing and singing and things like that. I can't really remember um when I was in Philly like you know who was the funniest or best guy that went up and sang. Um but I do remember it happening when I was there in Philly and um you know I I think uh we had like Barkley and Z my second year in Philly that came in and and they that was the rookie class but yeah I can't really remember that stuff too too well but I know it was happening. I got lucky for sure. How about when it comes to Chip Kelly? He's a pretty interesting character. Do you have a memorable Chip Kelly story that you could share? >> Yeah. Um nothing nothing too interesting really except just he really had my back, you know. Um when things were were hard, I made mistakes or um you know, even simple things like he wanted to see certain things for me, he always came and vocalized it. you know, he never really was harsh about it. He just came and talked to me. I'll be maybe in warm-ups, you know, come over. Hey, Mo, you know, on this specific play, you know, I want to see you, etc., etc. So, I really appreciated how he handled me. Um, I think I became a vet quicker. He didn't baby me, nothing like that. He was just very objective. He was a straight shooter with me. Um, and so I appreciated that and it helped me just realize like like I said earlier, like I got a vouch for myself and um, I can't expect any handouts, you know, I wasn't really expecting any, but just kind of having that reinforced from how people were talking to me in that building. Um, I think that came down from Cha Kelly. Um, and I really appreciated that. But he was a cool dude, man. Really cool guy. Great public speaker. You know, I'll say he's he could really get guys to buy into a program in a system. It was unfortunate to see how things ended for him in Philly. I think he could have been a great coach um you know as a coach and not so much as a as a manager, you know, general manager moving people around. I think he should have stuck to the coaching, but um what do I know? Like I think he was he did a great job um early on and really appreciate him giving me a chance. But I wish I had a cool story. I don't I do not have any unique or cool stories about Chip. But after your two summers in Philadelphia, you spend some time with the Cleveland Browns and the Detroit Lions, but how do you then land on your feet with the Arizona Cardinals? >> Yeah. Um unique situation. Um it was the first year and the last year um in 2015 that they 2015 offseason they did a veteran combine. Um not sure if you heard of that, but 2015 it was a unique time. They invited a hundred vets [clears throat] that were free agents, [cough] veterans that were free agents, excuse me, to come out and work out um in Arizona at that uh the Cardinal facility and the the coaches meetings were happening in Arizona that year, I believe. So, um it kind of worked out well where there were a ton of coaches, a ton of scouts, like a ton. It was really cool. um some really unique players, you know, I think Michael Sam and Felix Jones and uh trying to think who else. There were some bigname players, you know, that that were there um that worked out. And um it was it was really good because at that time I was a free agent and I had just got cut by the Lions because of an injury that I didn't disclose to them. Um and ended up going down to see Dr. Andrews in Florida and word got back to to the lines and they cut me in in uh in February and in March I did the workout did well enough to have it was Pittsburgh, Minnesota, and Arizona looking to sign me as a tight end. It's the first year I officially declared I was a tight end and um I went with the Cardinals, you know, gut feeling. I absolutely fell in love with what um Bruce Arens was standing for. Um the things he was telling me, wasn't selling me a dream, just telling me how he had a plan. Um, and then the icing on the cake after my veteran uh combine workout. I had Carson Palmer texting me like, "Hey Mo, you know, I heard great things about you. I had a chance to watch a little bit of your film. I think you'd be a great fit for us." And so I really felt the the love that I could come and play and make a impact on the team to help them win. And I went with the Cardinals and that's kind of how that that journey started where I started to have some real success in the NFL. >> So they were all looking at you as a tight end. >> Yeah. Yeah. all those teams and and like I said, it was the first year I officially declared, you know, hey, I'm not a receiver anymore. I'm a tight end. And I put some weight on. I got went from 230 to about 255 and two 250. And the heaviest I weighed while I was playing was about 260. So, >> and what did that diet and training regimen consist of to get to that weight? >> Oh man. Um, it just upped up and heavy loaded the the calorie intake. Um, you know, I thought I would enjoy it. I definitely didn't, you know, there's no worse feeling than, you know, force-feeding yourself to put weight on. Um, but I would say majority of the time I felt like, um, I was pretty hungry and I was on a good diet. I, um, utilize the Cardinals dietitionian. Um, she helped me get set up with a meal plan where I was getting food delivered to my house. Um, and of course, just tracking my, uh, you know, my calorie intake and things of that nature. you know, slow burn situation, not you know, a sprint, not all at once. I was trying to do it slow. So, um yeah, it was tough, but but you know, it it worked out. How satisfying was it for you, Fonnie, to get on the field and and have, you know, be able to to leave your imprints on the game a little bit and and close that chapter? >> It was cool. It was it was a great feeling. Um especially just having a chance to play against some teams that I felt like I had a a vendetta against. You know, I'm from New York. I'm a Long Islander. I grew up a Giants fan. Um uh and so we had the chance to play the Giants. Had a good game against them. Um and the same went for the 49ers at that time. Um might be mistaken, but I think so. So Kelly went from Philly to the Niners for a little bit. >> Right. Yeah. >> Yeah. Um and and so did Coach Day. Coach Day was there as well. And you know, like I said, Chip Kelly treated me great. um no ill will towards him at all, you know, but you know, it was a chance to hey, you should have kept me in Philly. And so I had a really good game against uh the 49ers that first year with the Cardinals as well. Forced a fumble, helped us win the game on kickoff and a couple catches, too. So, um yeah, I would say that, you know, just that, you know. Yeah. >> Well, at what point did you realize that either you were done with the game or the game was finished with you? >> Yeah. Um, my third year in Arizona, um, I think it was week 10, Thursday night football game against Seattle. Um, I [clears throat] ended up getting rolled up on after a Peterson and a defensive tackle landed on my on my leg. I was I was blocking and the play happened behind me. So kind of got flung forward and my foot stayed in the ground and so I broke my leg, dislocated ankle, um bunch of ligaments torn and you know had had multiple surgeries and um after about 16 months after that injury um I just you know and I I sat back and just considered everything that had happened, right? My third year in the NFL was my first year with the Cardinals and that first year with the Cardinals I got put on IR the first day of the regular season after I tore miniscus and the second year I made it six weeks in or something like that and broke my hand and had two surgeries that offseason and the third year is when I had this significant injury. So you know I sat back after you know all those surgeries and after some time and just thought like you know I could continue down this path and keep pushing and seeing what I can do. Um, and also at the same time risk, you know, another significant injury. I felt very poorly with my knees, my ankles, everything was kind of just in a bad place. Um, and so with those those thoughts and where I was at, talked to my family, I just decided like, hey, you know, there's a lot more to what I want to do with my life than just football. I love the game. I really appreciate everything it gave to me. Um, but I think I'm ready to hang the cleats up and just, you know, pursue the next step. I got a lot out of football, a lot out of what I was doing with the NFL. um super grateful and you know I felt like it helped propel me into you know life now what what I'm doing now but of course if I can go if you know I think about all the time you maybe I should have kept pushing and you know I remember that what really happened what pushed me over the edge was I think it was month 15 after my surgery and I got released by the Cardinals or yeah Cardinals and month 15 after my surgery I got a call from the Lions and they flew me in and did a physical and I failed the physical cuz of my ankle and that was it you know I was like I interest, but like I'm feeling physicals. I feel my body like I'm I'm in pain. It's hard for me to, you know, to to get down some stairs, you know, just with that the way, you know, my meniscus and both my knees are and stuff and my ankle. So, just felt like it was time to hang it up and and move on. So, >> did you already have a next step in mind for the post football career? >> Yeah. Yeah, I did. I while I was playing, I completed my masters. I got my NBA. Um, and I always knew I wanted to get involved in just player representation in some capacity. I had no idea about the college stuff, NIL, things like that that was coming um, years down the line. Maybe working as a scout, you know, some kind of front office position or something in the world of like working at the NFL or NFLPA offices. I did that for a little while and that's kind of that was like the first thing I did and got me set up um, on my way to work in this space of player representation where I work now. >> Well, let's bring your story current. um what exactly are you doing currently? Where are you working and and all that? >> Yeah, so yeah, 2019 that's when I was working with the NFLPA. Um like I said, I did that for about a year and a half. Um right up until about when COVID hit. Um and when COVID hit, you know, I figured, you know, I had some great experience at the PA. I [clears throat] really I had the chance to learn about the CBA. the CBA had gone through a renewal. Um, and really cool opportunity to be around a bunch of lawyers. Um, great people at in that building. I wanted to dabble into [clears throat] the player representation space more kind of hands-on in a more hands-on aspect. So, I went and worked for a company called Rubicon Talent based in New York City. Um, they're a talent marketing agency. Um, I'm not sure if you heard of like Titan University. >> Oh, yeah. Yeah. >> Like that. there they they're George KD and Greg Olsson's agent marketing agency. So I worked there for about a year. Um the year that we started Tiny University, I was there boots on the ground with the three guys that started it, Travis, Kelsey, um KD, and Olsen. Um and um you know my my my goal there my objectives were to focus on this new NIL um landscape that was coming because at that time that's when um a lot of the legal space was starting to to come into effect and different um legal cases were being heard and you know the instit was under a ton of pressure and you know things were changing. Um, so with Rubicon, I was tasked with creating the NIL division there and just recruiting players and learning a ton about hands-on marketing for for big-time players, right? I was working with the 1enters in locker rooms. Um, and really really cool lucrative deals were happening. So, I really appreciated that experience and um, you know, I just didn't I knew it wasn't really for me. I wanted to go on work with guys who were more like myself, right? guys that weren't the first round draft pick or day one draft picks. Guys that really had talent and knew they wanted to be more than just a football player, but were giving 110% of themselves in football and in something else. Like that's like my cup of tea. I want to help those guys like help guys like that make it and also establish themselves in their in their lives, not just in football, but like hey, let's get a plan here from the day that you signed us contract. you know, we already worked up a plan and we know what's going to happen as far as on the field, off the field, and life after after football. So, I left Tubercan after a year and a half and joined a company called The XL Sports Management. It's actually my college roommates's agency. Um, he and I both got our NBAs at the same time and that's where we really bonded and connected and we stayed in touch the entire time from when I left Boston College up until I joined 3XL. Um, he actually helped me when I was in the NFL to get a water deal and get a Nike deal. And that was kind of like another moment where I was like, I I want to do the work that he's doing. I want to settle up and partner up with him. So, you know, after the full circle from BC up until I left Rubicon, um, I joined 3XL. Um, and I've been there for about three years now. Um, just got certified last summer as a as a on the field NFL onfield agent. So, um, I have, uh, you know, five clients that I signed and one guy made it, got signed with the Jets, Malik, um, Malik Mlan out of Arizona State and, um, excited for his opportunities. Um, so that's what I'm doing in the working world. And I'm also a semester away from graduating from ASU Law School. So, you know, keep myself busy. Thank you, man. I appreciate that. Keep myself busy. Um, and just continuing to chase after goals, man. You know, I think the mindset from football never really leaves. And I always just feel like, you know, when I wake up, I want to be challenging myself and pushing towards something. And um, yeah, I feel like I've set myself up to to keep doing that. Just try to affect change and help out the next generation as far as the guys who are like myself, football players, hungry for football, hungry for other things in life. Um, check those boxes and, you know, pay it forward. Um, and that kind of helps me stay motivated and keep pushing to, you know, be a better version of myself every day. >> Hey, Philly fans, game day is stressful enough. Top quality cannabis, great prices, and an experience made for Philly fans 21 and up. >> It's a great story, man. And was is your recent endeavor inspired by your experience as a player? >> Say that one more time. >> Your recent endeavor, what you're doing now, was that at all influenced by, you know, you your playing career and some of the things you experienced there? >> Sure. Yeah. Yeah. the the [clears throat] catalyst to law school, well I won't say catalyst, the catalyst to law school was my time at the NFLPA and working on the CBA. But the first thought I had about going to law school was when I tore my ACL. And you know, I played as a true freshman. I played as a as a as a um excuse me, I played as a true freshman, played as a true sophomore, and then red shirted my junior year because of my injury. Um I sprained my MCL in training camp. Missed about seven, eight weeks. Halfway through the season, I could have come back from it. I tried and I just didn't feel healthy. I didn't feel good and the coaches wanted to sit me. So, I red shirted. Um, and then I tore my ACL red shirt senior year, appealed for a sixth year. And the NCAA said that I do not qualify because that first injury, my red shirt junior year, which would have been my true junior year. Um, that first injury wasn't a season ending injury that I could have came back from it and played another four games. Um, and I didn't have a notice in there saying like, hey, he's out for the season because of the injury. even though, you know, I I didn't feel healthy. But anyways, long story short, I just didn't like that appeal process. I I got tied up in the bylaws. I was reading it, highlighting, like talking to my family like, "Well, this thing says this." And going back to compliance at Boston College, having meetings with them, multiple meetings. And, you know, I got super close with the um with the head of compliance for Boston College. Um Carly, I still talk to her to this day because of that process. And when I got turned away, I just felt like it was BS and the laws were written poorly and I wanted to to change them. you know, I felt like I wanted to be a politician at that time. And the energy and the experiences that I gained from that situation up until, you know, you know, I applied for law school, you know, everything really kind of pointed me in a direction of like I do want to be able to understand the legal space. Um I want to get a stronghold understanding and handling of you know how lawyers um create laws people that are stakeholders in that space how they go about creating the things that are binding and controlling on what people real people can do whether it's in football or anything and um you know maybe be able to now after I'm you know completing law school and and bar certified can actually go out and affect change in a way that's truly you know meaningful and very impactful in a deeper way. Um, but college, that sixth year being denied, that that really set me down this path of of where I'm at and kind of kind gave me a little insight and a little kickstart into going down and doing what I'm doing now. >> Well, there's something there's some things uh throughout your story that I think everyone can take and apply to their own life. And on top of everything else, whenever there's a 6'6 or a 6'7 wide receiver in Eagles camp, they tend to draw comparisons to Afani Mom. Just so you know, your name is still talked about to this day. >> Let me tell you, man. I I know because I have a Twitter and people are always tagging me right around July 21st or, you know, somewhere in that time. And what can you share about Darius that the fan base should know? >> I would say this, you know, the first time that I met Darius, um I knew the guy was the real deal. And I'm not talking about the football player. I'm talking about the man. You know, he's a very very serious guy. He takes himself seriously and um that mindset that he has about, you know, business and carrying himself and handling himself as a as a business and, you know, taking care of the things that need to be taken care of. um him and his wife um they're very much so, you know, going in the right direction with how they're carrying themselves and pursuing the different goals that they have set out for themselves in their lives. Um and then the film, you know, watching him play in college is it was unreal. The kid is a baller. I knew he was going to make it. I knew he was going to make some noise when he, you know, got the helmet and pads on um wherever he went. Um and I think it starts with the man off the fields. you know, he just has the right head on his shoulders and that's a testament to the people that raised him and, you know, the work that he put in. Um, so yeah, he he's just he's just a kind of guy that, you know, you just want to you you want to be around, you want to learn from as he goes down this path of his NFL career and becomes a vet. I'm excited to see what he accomplishes and, you know, the different people he impacts, not just on the field as a player, but also in those locker rooms and, you know, around the league, cuz that's the kind of guy he is. you know, he's he's uh he has that contagious energy, you know, just putting people in a good mood and and um and carrying himself the right way. So, >> I started paying attention to him very early on in training camp, and one thing that really struck me was his business-like approach every day. He was looking at it as almost like every day you have to prove yourself. And he made a play every single day. And it was very apparent about halfway through camp that he belongs and he's going to make this football team. >> For sure. For sure. And it was really cool to see him get those opportunities throughout the season as a rookie. You know, like I said, it's hard for anybody that goes into the NFL or any professional sport to make an impact right away um and have the the right mentality. title: Football at Four: DiCecco's Look at the NFL's AFC East
text: Football 4 powered by the Inside the Birds podcast, which you can get on all podcasting platforms. It's the start of our divisional previews, the AFC East. Lot of storylines. When we get to the divisional previews, you know we are [music] kicking into high gear. The NFL is almost here. Andrew DiCecco is here and the AFC East has a ton of storylines. We're going to get into them right now on the Sports Bash Live as we welcome back Andrew DiCecco for today's Football at 4. What's up, man? How are you? >> Hey Mike, doing great. Good to be with you. >> As always, we've got the divisional previews, which means we're counting down to the start of training camp here and we start with the AFC East this week and I guess one of the big stories last season was the New England Patriots. Mike Vrabel, we know the off-the-field stuff. He's now year two at the helm, 14 and three. They go to the Super Bowl. They get A.J. Brown. What do you think is the big kind of story for New England? Is it, hey, them winning the AFC East last year and repeating or do you think all this off-the-field Vrabel stuff and A.J. Brown coming over there will dominate when they get to training camp? >> Well, inevitably, that's going to follow them, but eventually that should dissipate and then it becomes all about football because the focus in September just that that that's just when the dust settles, that's just it comes to the forefront and I think for the Patriots, when you look at how the season ended for them in the Super Bowl, it didn't go as expected. They fell on their face. I'm sure that Drake May, their young quarterback, is going to look for redemption this year. There's questions out there as to whether or not they are a team that's primed for a regression. That's a little unfounded to me. I still think anytime you add a premier wide receiver to a team that's already pretty well rounded, I think that puts you in a pretty good spot to do some damage. Now, Super Bowl, I'm not there yet. We have to wait and see what the product looks like on the field, but I do like some of their additions and Drake May is a player that it's been fun to watch his ascent. >> Yeah, Drake May obviously went from, you know, questionable questioned draft choice of what he would be. Where do you look at him now? I mean, is he He was in the MVP conversation last year. >> Yeah, I I think he's going to almost pick up where he left off. When you add AJ Brown, you add Romeo Dobbs from the Green Bay Packers. Elijah Vera-Tucker comes in at guard for them, adds a little bit more stability there to their offensive line. And they drafted Caleb Lomu in the first round. They have a lot of pieces and you couple that then with the running game, which alleviates some of the pressure with Ramondre Stevenson, Treyvion Henderson. And I don't know, I I think that's an offense that's going to be able to support a pretty high-octane passing game and that that's really his bread and butter, throwing the football and pushing it down the field, taking some chances. And AJ Brown, I believe, is going to be the immediate beneficiary of this of a byproduct of this offense. >> Yeah, you you wonder how drastically does AJ Brown and then he's in Josh McDaniels, the passing concepts. How does it kind of take Does it take May to another level? >> I believe it will. And like I go back to what I was saying, anytime you add You look at what Drake May did last season with a very underwhelming cast of wide receivers who were really, I mean, you had Diggs, but apart from that, they were really twos and threes. You've added a top 10 wide receiver. I don't do the rankings, but he's pretty damn elite in AJ Brown. And he's going to be motivated. Drake May and that whole team is going to be motivated. There's a lot of noise right now around their organization that was self-inflicted, of course, but I just get the sense that they're going to look to prove something early and quiet some of that noise and most notably A.J. Brown. >> Uh Andrew Checker, we're looking at the uh New England Patriots. A lot of people look at them and say byproduct of the schedule, schedule much more difficult. Um what move kind of stands out? You said you like some of the moves. Obviously A.J. Brown is at the top of that list. Uh Lomo who they drafted in the first round. Uh what's a reason why we think this team is more than just the schedule they had last year? >> Well, I like another year another year of Milton Williams who I thought had a really good season. Uh they added Draymond Jones, Gabe Jackson in the second round. He's a pass rusher. They've added some more depth there. Uh Kevin Byard, uh of course former Eagles safety for a short period of time uh comes over to team with Craig Woodson. Craig Woodson one of the more underrated safeties in the game. Was a fourth-round pick in 2025. Marcus Jones at nickel. So all of these players are are sort of just going to continue to grow within that system. And then I looked at the offense and it was evident that prior to acquiring A.J. Brown, they needed a a a a bonafide playmaker at the receiver position. They got that. Now do I think that they're suddenly going to uh have another surge towards a a deep postseason run? Well, that that remains to be seen, but they are going to be a competitive football team. And I'm not one that subscribes to the notion that they're going to take a dramatic step back just because, you know, the law of averages tells you that it it's tough to repeat or or replicate the success that you had. >> All right, let's go to the Buffalo Bills who obviously had been running that division for a little while here. They made a coaching change. Joe Brady is now the head coach. New uh Jim Leonards in there. He'll run the defense here. So you're getting a new look. Uh is this what Buffalo needed? Did they need this coaching change? >> I think so. Every once in a while the messaging can get stale and with Sean McDermott, he's a good football coach, but and and I don't fault him for he he was part of the reason why they were never able to quite get over the hump, but not the sole reason, but it's a lot easier to swap out your head coach. But Mike, they they've added some good pieces. DJ Moore at wide receiver in that trade and that now complements what they have in Khalil Shakir. Maybe takes a little bit of pressure off of him cuz I thought he was a little miscast as being a predominant option. Keon Coleman, a second-round pick in 2024 is someone who still needs to prove himself. He's flashed a little bit. James Cook, a a a very dynamic player at running back. You have, of course, Josh Allen who makes everything go, one of the most valuable players in the NFL. And they even added a former Eagle at fullback, and that would be one Ben Van Ben Van Sumeren. >> Ben Van Sumeren, yes, the guy who had the injury here last year. You wonder what kind of impact he may have had had he got an opportunity to really I mean, that was kind of an underrated that injury they had on on opening night there. TJ Parker, >> horrible. Yeah, it was a horrible injury and he would have had, to be clear, he would have had a role here in Philadelphia had it not been for the injury. And just a really athletic player, one of the best athletes when he was on the Eagles and yeah, that was something that when you and I talked about this, Mike, not having him and Johnny Wilson, it doesn't necessarily show up in the box score, but two guys who do the dirty work. >> Absolutely, and they did not have a first-round pick last year. We were just talking TJ Parker, you know, the edge rusher from Clemson. They went with a corner in the second round. They had two second-round picks. Is that defense up to the test? It was a big problem for them. >> Yeah, really. They weren't able to pick up the tab. The offense was tasked with a lot, but you you've you have players who I like who's returning in T.J. Sanders. He was a second round pick in 2025. And Al Woods has been a mainstay on that defense. Greg Rousseau as a pass rusher, I don't think he gets enough love from a national perspective. Christian Benford is a really good story development as a sixth round pick in 2022 at one cornerback spot. C.J. Gardner-Johnson is now with the Buffalo Bills if you're having trouble keeping up with where he where he is these days. And we'll see what that what happens there. I do like their safety tandem in Cole Bishop who was a second round pick in 24 and Gardner-Johnson. Jeff Hafley is the new head coach there. Kind of an unknown if you're wondering where where did this guy come from? He was the Packers assistant. They promoted promoted Bobby Slowik. He is now the offensive coordinator. So, you've got a new coordinator, new head coach, new defensive coordinator. This is a team that had had Tua for years. They put big money into Willis down there. Adding someone like Malik Willis who you haven't necessarily seen enough from him to to generate a ton of buzz, but there's intrigue there and you wonder what he can do with a full complement of games to work off of and grow from. Cayden Proctor, who the Eagles liked in this draft, was their first-round pick. He looks like he's going to play some guard for them early. Jaylen Twyman is someone who with the Dallas Cowboys you saw flashes, but you didn't see a lot of consistency there, but I think in maybe a different situation he can thrive. I really liked him coming out of South Alabama. Chris Bell, a third-round pick for them. He's probably a first-round pick if he doesn't have the knee injury at Louisville in his final season. That was a tremendous value. We'll have to wait and see how early he's going to be able to help them. And Achane, they have Jaylen Wright. So, they have some dynamic playmakers on that side of the ball. The big question, and it's a fair one, and it's a pretty big one, what are they getting in Malik Willis? Who is Malik Willis? >> Two first-round picks, Cayden Proctor, the offensive tackle, a top 15 pick. Uh he went number 12. Chris Johnson, the corner on defense. title: Mike Florio reacts to 'stunning' results from NFL study | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: This came up yesterday and look I think that it is important. I mentioned this as it relates to Chris Johnson last week. I mentioned it as it relates to Marshon Neland and the determination that he had stage one the lowest of four levels of CTE. Neandall died by suicide in November of 2025. Family donated the brain for research by Boston University's experts. study came out yesterday and it's similar to a study that emerged in 2021 regarding the risk of developing ALS. That was something I mentioned last week. I noticed some of the same doctors involved in both studies and it's roughly the same number of participants 19,000 and change players who were studied who played at least one game in the NFL from 1960 through 2019. So it's basically the same group from 5 years ago. The finding was that the risk of developing ALS is four times greater for anyone who's played in the NFL at least one game from 1960 through 2019 than it is for the general population. Yesterday's study very different. Yesterday's study looks at the mortality risk, the death risk from neuro degenerative disease for anyone who played at least one NFL game from 1960 through 2019. And it's somewhere between three and four times greater, which isn't surprising to those of us who have been following for the past, hell, it's 17 years now. The NFL's epiphany about concussions was forced upon it in October of 2009 when both the commissioner and then NFL PA executive director Demora Smith were called to Congress for a hearing and the message was clear. You got a problem. You better clean it up or we're going to clean it up for you. And that's when they embarked on the effort to clean it up by taking the blows to the head to the extent to which we used to see them out of the game. And there have been many changes. It's been very slow. But if you go back and watch, and there's plenty of old games on YouTube from the 80s and the '9s, very different game. Very different game. The level of physicality, the guys getting blown up across the middle when they catch a pass, blows to the head, hits with the helmet. They've done what they can to change it. There's only so much you can do. But we are at the point now, 17 years later, where those of us who follow it carefully realize that there is a connection between not just concussions, but what they call subconussive trauma where you're just coming off the line and if you're an offensive lineman, your helmet crashes into the helmet of a defensive player. for both guys. They may not suffer a concussion and the vast majority of time they don't, but it's that blow to the head that doesn't concuss the brain, but they accumulate over time, over time, over time. And it resulted in this finding. And in comparison to the general population, it is stunning. And here's another thing that makes it even more dramatic. This is a point that was made in the summary of the research that was sent out yesterday. The mortality rate for NFL players when you take in all causes is lower than the general population. And they've realized that and I'm going to keep this very very simple because it's the limit of my ability to explain it and understand it. But basically the thing that makes them elite athletes, they are elite physical specimens. They take care of themselves. The things that people who don't have the genetics, the work ethic, the work product of years and years and years of constantly doing what you can to take care of your body. Those folks are going to as they get older, they're going to die of the things that the foundation for which are laid when you're young and you're not working out and taking care of yourself the way that professional athletes do. So for all causes, the death rate is lower. And as they point out in the summary of the research effort, it makes this spike for mortality arising from neurogenerative diseases like ALS, Parkinson's, dementia, etc. It makes it even more alarming because for all other reasons, football players are a lot healthier and they live longer. But in this one area, the death rate four times higher. I went back and forth with some people yesterday about this because look, my position is we now know the risks and we need to make sure that the players who are signing up to play now know the risks. And I'll agree. I'll stipulate, as the lawyers would say, that there are plenty of guys who have played in recent years who weren't told the full range of the risks. So, they weren't able to make the same kind of cleareyed decision that players nowadays can make. And that's unfortunate because the first decision that's made is just to play football at all. And the parents are involved in that. And there was a time 2012 2013 where the participation rate in youth football began to dramatically decrease. High school teams were shrinking. That's changed to a certain extent and the NFL pays close attention to that because your supply of future NFL players is driven by how many are playing. It's just like I was saying yesterday about soccer. You got to have enough people playing so that the best will emerge and be tested against good competition and gradually get better and better and better and by the time they finish their college careers, they're a completed product ready to compete and make the roster and and contribute at a high level to an NFL team. So, I just think it's fair for everybody to know the risks. I I'm not here to throw stones at the failure of the NFL, college football, anyone to point out all the risks in years past. Was there a time where the NFL covered up the risks? Yes, that's documented. They downplayed the risks and the NFL PA had a seat at the table. That was one of the big problems I had with the League of Denial book. And I have a copy of it because I wanted to see do they ever mention when the NFL set up in 1994 the mild traumatic brain injury committee which basically became the mechanism for downplaying the risks of head trauma. The NFLPA always had a seat at the table and the NFLPA is the players. Now, of course, the players don't ultimately run it. They're not sitting at the very top, but the NFL PA had a seat at the table, and that was something that was glossed over completely in the initial effort to point out the NFL's failures when it comes to being transparent and honest about the risk head trauma. And even if they had been, the vast majority of guys who played would have still played. I think it's more of a PR thing. And at its core, I think underlying everything is this fear that the pool of players is going to shrink. And I've seen it argued that, well, it really doesn't matter if the pool shrinks because it's only a small percentage that makes it to the NFL. But that overlooks the reality of how this works. You need to have that pool in order to ensure that the guys who occupy the small percentage are in that pool and not playing baseball or basketball or soccer. So I think it's important to point it out and let me point out one more thing before I move on. I saw something unawatted Jr. who is one of the traditional journalists employed by ESPN. He recently got a new contract and he was saying somewhere that this shows ESPN's commitment to journalism. And that's fine, but I think that with the NFL now owning 10% of ESPN, the focus shouldn't be the macro. Do they still have traditional journalists on staff? Are they still doing traditional journalism that may may reflect poorly on the NFL or any of its teams? The macro, it would be too obvious if that went away. The micro is what we need to look at. I've mentioned before that there was an unflattering report about the circumstances surrounding the off-field issues involving James Pierce Jr. or the Falcons and ESPN posted that right as the floodgates were opening for free agency. It it just disappeared. It just was lost. So yeah, they did the work. They engaged in the journalism, but it was published at a time where no one was going to notice it. the the one lengthy article that I can remember about the whole Mike Vrabel, Diana Rousini thing, it was published late on a Friday afternoon and it didn't come with the car wash we used to see where the person would publish the article and then you'd see the author on this show, this show, this show, this show. And they used to they used to be very strategic in the timing of when they would drop these stories. I think that's one thing that we need to watch. We need to watch the little things when these stories emerge, where, when, and how aggressively are those stories marketed? Is it just a box that's being checked so no one will say, "Well, they've they've stopped engaging in journalism." It's not whether or not they are, but how they're packaging it, how they're marketing it, where they're putting it, when they're putting it. And I mention all that I don't see anything. As of the last time I checked on ESPN about this study that came out yesterday, not a word. Now they had a story about the Marshon Neland CTE diagnosis postumously. They've had things pre merger with NFL about issues of this nature. I'm going to give them a few more hours. I'm probably going to write something about it at PFT. But this is one of the little things. Yeah. They still have journalists. Yeah. And every once in a while there's going to be a big splash article, it's fair to watch the little things because the league owns 10% of it now. 10% of the whole operation. Hi, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Hit subscribe for the latest news and analysis from Pro Football

title: Kelsey Pfendler recounts her harrowing solo row across the Pacific Ocean 😱 | SportsCenter
text: Over the course of 43 days and some odd hours, Kelsey Fendler captured our attention by becoming the first American woman to row solo from California to Hawaii, like row, row, row your boat. A 2400 mile journey in which she absolutely smashed records and probably ate more peanut butter than any one person should be allowed to consume. alone over open waters through storms, quiet nights, and nothing to really occupy her but her thoughts and maybe some music and a hell of a lot of hope and guts to inspire women everywhere because yes, we can do hard things. And I'm not kidding, Kelsey. I have been looking forward to this moment since I think I discovered your journey. So, first of all, thank you for for joining us. >> Uh, congratulations. How are you feeling? Thank you for saying that because that is kind of the whole point is if I can get some women to feel excited about doing their own hard stuff. Like that's the entire point of this. So I um I'm feeling so many things right now. I think it's still uh taking a little time to process everything that's happened. Um I've been really busy, so I haven't really gotten the chance to really reflect on like the fact that this this all came to pass. I didn't int well I didn't even think it was possible to break the men's record coming into this. So it's still a thing that um I'm still kind of telling myself happened and I still think I have to remind myself that this this just happened. >> Yeah. Cuz you didn't set out to necessarily set a record. You wanted to make sure that you could do this yourself as an individual >> in the women's record. >> In the women's record, but all that other stuff came after. So again, as you sort of sit with your accomplishment, what has maybe amazed yourself about yourself the most? Honestly, I think the I knew that I could go on a little sleep, but the the utter lack of sleep that I was able to function on was pretty interesting to me cuz I um I didn't know how that was all going to go. Like I had a pretty big plan um in the beginning for the first week to try to see how far I could get with almost no sleep because the first week is really challenging um getting off the coast and when you're sleeping as a solo that's when you're the most vulnerable and all the currents and wind and wave direction usually push you either south or back towards the shore for at least the first week or the first like 300 miles getting off the um the continental shelf. So, my plan was to sleep as little as possible. And I was really only sleeping like an hour a day um that first week and a half. And then the rest of the trip I was only sleeping 4 hours a day in like maybe 2 hour segments. >> And I was able to actually function a lot better than I thought I was going to on that little amount of sleep. And my body actually like really adjusted. And that was something that was really surprising to me. >> How were you able to function at all, Kelsey, with so little sleep? and then do something so physically demanding. I'm I am in awe of this. >> Bodies are amazing. I mean, honestly, and I think um I I do believe that women are really good at endurance sports. We're super capable of dealing with pain and um emotional regulation under stress. And I think just like what a body can do is we don't even know honestly. Like every year in the Olympics, people push the boundaries even further. So it's it's really hard to tell what a person can really do because every year in sports people go past the perceived limit. So >> but this is >> I don't know. I think it's it's really capable. >> This is more than going past a perceived physical limit. You probably went past some some mental limits as well. >> So how did you how did you train for this and how did you train for both aspects of this journey? Well, I came off of a So, I did a row in 2024 with a team of three other women um to Kawaii, Hawaii. Um so, I came off that row knowing that I was going to do another row and I I didn't have a concrete plan of what that was going to look like initially, but I came to realize that I really wanted to do a solo and I wanted to do the same route. So, I I came off the back of a hard row of the same route and just kind of continued the training. So, I was already in a good spot to just keep moving forward towards the next row. Um, I had to get a little bit stronger. I did a lot of powerlifting, obviously, a lot of rowing, um, to get my strength back. Um, and then the sleep stuff, you know, like obviously I was super sleepd deprived on my first row, but I'm also I work in an ER, um, and I do night shifts in the hospital as well. And, um, so I do I already do a lot of stuff at night, not sleeping very very much. So, I think I just came to realize you can do a lot with very little sleep. Does it is it always good for you? Probably not. No. >> But you can do it and you just have to >> you just you can work through it. And it's more of like the story you tell yourself if you're fine or not. Um and what you can move yourself through. >> Okay. I could have this conversation for a very long time and I I have a list of questions that I I really want to get to. One of the things that struck me though after you did get to land and after you were celebrated by your team and people who didn't know you, you had a video where you came out and said, "I was surprised by how overwhelming it was to be surrounded by people again after 43 days and some odd hours at sea." So, what has surprised you the most about being back on land and being with people again? I mean, it it definitely was just very overwhelming to go from like that much isolation. Um, I really wasn't in contact with people very often. I would turn on my Starlink maybe like 20 minutes out of the day um to send videos and check the weather. Um, and I wasn't really doing a lot other than rowing. So going from that isolation to then the amount of people that were there and everyone was so kind, but there were so many people um at the yach club that I uh landed at because I got there earlier than expected. At first we thought we were I was going to get there at like maybe 1 or 2 a.m. and it was going to be kind of quiet, but I got there at like 9:00 p.m. on one of the busiest days of the entire year for the yach club. So, there was just so many people there. And then there was a lot of people outside kind of just like yelling for me to come outside um that I I just I was so overwhelmed I ended up just hiding in like a storage room um with a couple people because I didn't know uh what to do in that moment. Um and it took a little bit of time to just like readjust and like talking to other humans standing in front of me was was kind of a lot at first. >> Eye contact gets weird again. >> Yeah. Right. I mean the isolation you got to be kind of a whole transition getting back to people and plus there were way more eyes looking at you than you were looking at eyes right so you felt I'm pretty sure like a spotlight I wonder >> during the course of that isolation Kelsey what were the darkest moments that you experienced I don't mean just dark in terms of lack of sunlight I mean just dark with along with your thoughts >> oh yeah I mean there were especially getting off the California coast I had a lot of fear and self-doubt and Um, there was a big storm that hit me kind of around day five that was really intense.
